candidates.title: Diffusion-enhanced GFlowNet for solving vehicle routing problems
candidates.abstract: Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models.However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes.The deeper exploration could yield superior results.Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration.These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration.Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward highreward regions and derive higher-quality solutions.Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet's inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm.To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales.Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods.The code is available at https://github.com/ZHANG-NI/DEG.Recent neural solvers for VRPs can be broadly categorized into Autoregressive (AR) and Non-Autoregressive (NAR) models.AR models, such as those based on pointer networks and Transformer 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).

candidates.title: Digital twin-driven multi-objective optimization of milling parameters under small-sample conditions
candidates.abstract: Abstract To address the high experimental cost, insufficient parameter-space coverage, and multi-objective trade-off difficulties in milling parameter optimization under small-sample conditions, this study proposes a digital twin-driven multi-objective optimization method for milling parameters. An end-milling process is considered, with spindle speed, feed rate, axial depth of cut, and radial depth of cut selected as input parameters. A unified virtual evaluation interface is constructed to rapidly evaluate machining time, cutting force, and the probability of satisfying surface quality constraints. To improve parameter-space coverage, a diffusion-inspired noise-perturbation augmentation method is used to generate supplementary samples, which are further filtered using parameter bounds and cutting-force physical consistency constraints. A Gaussian process regression model is then established as a surface roughness threshold classification model, transforming surface quality evaluation into a probabilistic constraint satisfaction problem. Based on the virtual evaluation model, Bayesian optimization and a multi-objective genetic algorithm are combined to search for Pareto non-dominated solutions. The case study shows that the proposed method can generate a relatively continuous set of trade-off solutions among machining time, cutting force, and surface quality feasibility, providing alternative parameter combinations for different machining preferences. The optimization results are further integrated into a digital twin visualization system for interactive comparison and decision support. The recommended parameter combinations still require further validation through physical machining experiments.

candidates.title: Optimal-transport flow matching for stochastic model ipdating
candidates.abstract: Deep generative models have attracted considerable attention as inference engines for stochastic model updating. Among these deep generative models, conditional flow matching offers a particularly efficient formulation, in which a continuous transport map from a latent distribution to the posterior is learned by regression against optimal-transport probability paths, avoiding both the invertibility constraints of normalising flows and the iterative denoising of diffusion models. However, its performance in engineering model updating has not been examined against an established baseline such as the Bayesian updating framework under controlled conditions. In this work, conditional flow matching is therefore assessed against the Bayesian model updating approach with transitional Markov chain Monte Carlo, in which the Bhattacharyya distance provides the approximate likelihood for the Bayesian approach. The two methods are assessed with respect to posterior fidelity, evaluated by statistical distances against the known ground truth and computational expenditure in model evaluations, with the offline training budget reported separately from the inference cost of each subsequent conditioning. A 3-DOF spring–mass system with uncertain stiffness parameters serves as the benchmark. Since the calibrated posterior constitutes the input description upon which subsequent reliability assessment depends, the accuracy and the marginal cost of the updating step both bear directly on reliability computations. In addition, the amortised nature of the learned transport map is discussed in this work, as it permits the posterior to be re-evaluated under new observations at negligible cost, which is a property of practical relevance to reliability assessment under sequentially acquired monitoring data.

candidates.title: Critical Assessments of Computational Hit-finding Experiments Challenge #4: Targeting the Tyrosine Kinase Binding Domain of the E3 Ligase Casitas B-Lineage Lymphoma Proto-Oncogene B, an Immuno-Oncology Target
candidates.abstract: Abstract The critical assessments of computational hit-finding experiments (CACHE) are prospective benchmarking exercises where small molecule ligands predicted for a nominated protein of interest are procured and tested experimentally. In CACHE #4, 23 participating teams each selected up to 100 compounds designed to bind the E3 ligase CBLB, an immuno-oncology target. The organizers released the first public structure of CBLB in complex with a known ligand at the outset of the challenge to enable the discovery of chemically novel molecules. Out of the 1688 compounds collectively predicted, ten compounds from nine participants showed some sign of activity (primary hits), but only two were convincingly confirmed (validated hits) across multiple biophysical binding assays and in subsequent analogs, and only one of them was chemically novel. The apparent difficulty of finding novel CBLB ligands, previously reflected by the chemical similarity of inhibitors from the patent literature, suggests that potent CBLB hit molecules were either rare in the screened commercial libraries, or that computational methods may have struggled to retrieve presumably present but weak ligands, or that the conformational dynamics of the binding site was not sufficiently accounted for. The successful method was strikingly atypical. Selection from a chemical binding similarity classifier followed by a random forest binding affinity predictor trained on inhibitors from the patent literature was refined using a diffusion-model binding pose predictor. The road to an ML-driven breakthrough in computational hit-finding can take unexpected turns. Which of these turns reveal novel horizons and which are mere distractions will best be investigated and answered collectively. The discovery in CACHE #4 of a novel series of CBLB ligands is not a trivial achievement and may inform medicinal chemistry efforts toward clinical candidates that complement immune checkpoint inhibition to elicit antitumor immune response in cancer patients.

candidates.title: A human‐in‐the‐loop Bayesian optimization framework for constraint‐aware bioprocess development
candidates.abstract: Abstract We present Pareto Front Guided Sampling (PFGS), a human‐in‐the‐loop (HiL) Bayesian Optimization (BO) framework that reformulates surrogate‐model predictions as a multi‐objective optimization problem, allowing domain knowledge to be added intuitively to any BO problem. PFGS addresses constrained optimization by treating the posterior probability of constraint satisfaction as an explicit Pareto objective, and robust optimization via a Monte Carlo estimate of expected lower‐confidence performance under input perturbations, capturing likely degradation. The multi‐dimensional Pareto front makes trade‐offs between predicted performance, model uncertainty, constraint satisfaction, and robustness visible through pairwise two‐dimensional projections on an interactive dashboard, allowing selection criteria to be refined as the model and objectives evolve. The framework is showcased on a eight‐dimensional in‐silico fed‐batch Chinese Hamster Ovary cell culture case study. We showed improved performance over BO when the expert has perfect domain knowledge; however, PFGS is not designed to outperform BO, but rather to present a HiL acquisition function framework.

candidates.title: Design of a multi-stage hybrid optimizer combining Bayesian and evolutionary algorithms for modeling and optimizing seizure-related information in EEG signals
candidates.abstract: The prediction of epileptic seizures from EEG signal analysis is modeled as a complex, high-dimensional, multi-objective optimization problem. In this study, we propose and design a novel multi-stage hybrid optimizer that integrates Bayesian optimization with a family of evolutionary and metaheuristic algorithms, including Genetic Algorithm (GA), Evolutionary Programming (EP), Evolution Strategies (ES), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), Artificial Bee Colony (ABC), and Harmony Search (HS).This optimizer is structured to operate across sequential stages of optimization, where each stage is designed to progressively refine the solution space by selecting the optimal subset of EEG channels and time blocks related to the preictal phase. The mathematical model aims to maximize the posterior probability of seizure occurrence while minimizing the temporal distance to the actual seizure, thus formulating a well-defined trade-off in the objective space. Unlike traditional methods, the proposed hybrid framework models and controls the optimization trajectory by combining the global exploration capability of evolutionary algorithms with the adaptive search of Bayesian optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that the optimizer successfully converges toward high-informational regions of EEG data that occur early in the preictal phase. A detailed performance comparison and sensitivity analysis further validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach, offering insights into the design of more generalizable hybrid optimizers for complex modeling tasks.

candidates.title: Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
candidates.abstract: We develop score-based generative models for time series and standard finite-dimensional data, building on the analytical computation of the expected signature of a new class of jump-diffusions, called entire sig-jump-diffusions. These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

candidates.title: From Generative Molecular Design to Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery.
candidates.abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced the early stages of drug discovery, which focus primarily on target evaluation and the design or identification of new active small molecules or biologics. Deep neural networks adapted from areas such as natural language processing and computer vision have provided novel opportunities for generative modeling and human-machine interactions. State-of-the-art AI models for generative molecular design have emerged, but remain only little understood so far. Furthermore, new computational systems are being devised rapidly that are expected to significantly transform the drug discovery landscape in the near future. These developments pose challenges to computer-aided drug discovery in various ways. In the following, we discuss these opportunities and challenges, with a focus on molecular design.

candidates.title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
candidates.abstract: Abstract Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

candidates.title: Large language model agents with simulation-trained surrogates retrieve multi-objective reservoir development plans from hierarchical knowledge graphs
candidates.abstract: Optimizing oilfield development is a high-dimensional, multi-objective decision problem: candidate plans must balance hydrocarbon recovery against economic return while satisfying operational constraints. Retrieval methods that rank evidence by textual or structural similarity cannot express such trade-offs or reject infeasible plans, whereas full-physics simulation is too costly to run inside an interactive search. We present PHARAOH, a framework in which a large language model agent retrieves development plans over a multi-resolution knowledge graph, guided by a simulation-trained surrogate model that estimates objectives such as ultimate recovery and net present value. The agent combines global anchoring with type-filtered hierarchical refinement and aggregates parallel search trajectories into a set of diverse recommendations; its policy is then distilled into a compact student model. PHARAOH screens and ranks candidates within a pre-built decision space rather than solving a continuous optimization problem. On PetroGraph, a benchmark built from three public reservoir simulation models, PHARAOH attains the best average performance among the compared baselines, improving Hit@1 by 8.8 and Recall@20 by 7.1 over a surrogate-guided non-agentic search. Full-physics re-simulation shows that 14 of 15 top-ranked plans satisfy the operational constraints, although near-boundary plans remain sensitive to surrogate error. The distilled 7B student retains about 85% of the teacher’s Hit@1 at a fraction of the inference cost. These findings are limited to three simulation benchmarks; field-scale validation remains future work.

candidates.title: FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching
candidates.abstract: Limit order book (LOB) simulators are most useful to practitioners when they combine realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and the ability to generalize beyond the instruments seen during training---properties that existing agent-based and deep generative simulators provide only partially. We present \textbf{FlowLOB}, a conditional \textbf{flow}-matching generator of \textbf{LOB} trajectories, trained on multiple Hong Kong Exchange (HKEX) symbols at three sampling frequencies ($0.1$s, $1$s, $10$s) in tick-relative representation that transfers to unseen instruments. Because flow and diffusion models admit a common formulation, we train both with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sample both through the same fixed-step ODE solvers, yielding a controlled comparison of sampling efficiency and fidelity. Flow matching attains its best quality with only $10$ ODE-solver steps, whereas diffusion needs many more function evaluations to approach the same fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over baselines, two learned and two agent-based models, in most distributional metrics at the two finer sampling frequencies. We evaluate counterfactual controllability with a distributional test that asks whether changing a scenario condition moves the generated statistic toward the corresponding real tail regime; FlowLOB satisfies this criterion in most tested settings. Both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot on a held-out symbol. We additionally conduct ablation studies on the network architecture and the learning rate.

candidates.title: K2V: Generative Keyframing For Physically Plausible Video Generation
candidates.abstract: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.

candidates.title: CROWN: Curated Repository of Well-Resolved Noncovalent Interactions
candidates.abstract: Abstract The usefulness of structural data sets for machine-learning models of protein–ligand recognition depends not only on their size, but also on how structural imperfections are handled. Existing resources typically trade structural rigor for scale. Recent data sets such as SPINDR improve large-scale structural data through systematic preprocessing, but restrictive inclusion criteria still discard much of the chemical and biological complexity represented in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Here, we present Curated Repository Of Well-resolved Noncovalent interactions (CROWN), a machine-learning–ready data set built around a repair-first curation philosophy: structural inconsistencies are corrected whenever this can be done without compromising experimental evidence at the binding interface, while filtering is reserved for cases that cannot be repaired conservatively. Starting directly from deposited PDB structures, CROWN resolves alternate conformers and connectivity errors, reconstructs complete interaction environments, repairs missing or nonstandard regions outside the binding pocket, assigns protonation states at physiological pH and applies constrained energy minimization using flat-bottomed restraints to relieve local strain while preserving experimentally supported geometry. This strategy yields 193,374 protein–ligand complexes spanning 81,606 PDB entries and 18,516 UniProt accessions, representing more than a 5-fold increase in both complex count and protein diversity relative to SPINDR while retaining a uniform structural representation. Rather than organizing the data set around sparsely available binding-affinity measurements, CROWN adopts a geometry-centric design in which the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms at the binding interface provides the primary source of information. On CASF-2016, CROWN-trained knowledge-based potentials achieved the highest scoring and ranking performance among five training resources, while matching PDBbind- and HiQBind-trained models in docking and screening and consistently outperforming SPINDR-trained counterparts. Together with multiaxis similarity annotations and a companion web interface, CROWN provides a scalable resource for scoring-function development, pose prediction, binder generation, ligand-conditioned protein design, and other structure-based machine-learning applications.

candidates.title: Stochastic multiscale reconstruction of Lagrangian turbulence via guided diffusion models
candidates.abstract: Lagrangian turbulence is characterized by intermittent, fat-tailed fluctuations and nontrivial correlations across temporal scales, making a quantitative description of its full multiscale probability distribution a longstanding challenge. A particularly important question is whether unresolved fine-scale fluctuations can be inferred from coarse-grained trajectory information. Here, we address this problem by sampling the conditional distribution of unresolved fluctuations using a diffusion-model prior conditioned on large-scale dynamics obtained through a wavelet-based coarse-graining of Lagrangian trajectories. Using tracer trajectories from direct numerical simulations of homogeneous and isotropic turbulence at $Re_λ\simeq 310$, we show that the reconstructed signals recover scale-dependent intermittent statistics, including high-order structure functions, flatness, and local scaling exponents, together with cross-scale temporal correlations between resolved and unresolved fluctuations. The method also reproduces the broad stochastic variability of intermittent acceleration fluctuations conditioned on the same coarse-grained trajectory, whereas Gaussian-process reconstructions in wavelet representation suppress rare events. Our results show that small-scale Lagrangian intermittency can be modeled as a non-Gaussian conditional stochastic process constrained by coarse-scale dynamics and quantitatively reproduced through data-driven generative sampling.

candidates.title: Generative molecular dynamics of Li-ion electrolytes conditioned on force-field energy and force
candidates.abstract: We generate all-atom molecular dynamics simulation structures of Li-ion battery electrolytes following from molecular centers of mass with a flow-matching model that reads the force field’s energy and its force at its own predicted structure. Molecular dynamics (MD) with a polarizable force field is the reference for electrolyte structure and transport, but each new formulation costs a full simulation. We train a two-stage generative model on around 45,000 NVT simulations of 69 species run with MU-PFF, an in-house polarizable force field. Stage 1 generates the molecules’ centres of mass (COMs) over time; Stage 2 rebuilds every atom from one frame’s COMs by flow matching on each molecule’s orientation, torsions and residual displacements. In the final Stage 2 model (EF), every network evaluation first predicts the clean structure, then computes the MU-PFF pair energy and its force there, and feeds both into the network’s first layer (physics self-conditioning). Read at the noisy intermediate state instead, the same forces were not used by the network (0.006 % of the loss). We validate with energies and with forces. The energy check scores generated against MD frames under the force field. The force check is the configurational temperature θ per degree of freedom, which is 1 for Boltzmann-distributed frames; we first confirm it on MD frames with induced dipoles (63 of 73 classes). Every decision rule was fixed before the run it decided. Against an otherwise identical control (SC), EF lowers the energy excess from +9.48 to +9.12 kJ/mol per molecule (paired difference −0.36, 95 % interval [−0.75, −0.27]; lower in 93 of 100 frames and in every energy term). A second training seed reproduces the gain (−0.48 [−0.70, −0.31]), with the seed-to-seed spread well below it, and on all 200 validation systems the difference is −0.53 [−0.66, −0.36]. EF lowers θ on raw frames in 40 of the 41 force-fieldconsistent rotation and torsion classes (median −16 %) and moves the carbonyl alignment toward Li+ closer to MD for every species. The gain is in molecular orientation, and it comes with the force: the same energy fed without its derivative (E) changes nothing measurable. It also holds on Stage 1’s generated centres of mass, at four of five Stage 1 step sizes and at every system size from 0.8× to 2.0×. Stage 1 itself, compared with MD on 23 systems, reproduces the density (within 0.3 % from composition alone), the Li+ shell and the positions of the COM g(r) peaks (median shift 0.00 nm over 740 species pairs), but its peaks are 12 % lower and its molecules diffuse 1.7–1.9 times faster than MD’s at its shortest step. Over 200 frames per system, every model reproduces MD’s Li+ solvation on MD’s own centres of mass, where the force’s effect on structure is mixed; on Stage 1’s, EF is closer to MD than E in 15 of 20 properties and further in none, within errors that are Stage 1’s. On 28 independently simulated systems containing 19 species unseen in training, the structure transfers. From the composition alone, Stage 1 gives MD’s density within 5 % in 23 of the 28 systems (median ×1.001) and the Li+ shell in the median (×0.98–1.00); on the systems’ MD centres of mass, Stage 2’s Li–O coordination is 4.5 % below MD’s and its torsion populations stay close (Jensen–Shannon divergence 0.025). The energy excess is +16.5 kJ/mol per molecule in the median (+3 to +70 across systems, below the in-distribution +9.1 in 8 of them); EF’s excess is lower than SC’s in 21 of the 28 systems, although the pooled test fixed in advance does not resolve the difference. Stage 1’s diffusion is 1.4 times MD’s in the median, but it pulls the least and most mobile systems toward the corpus’s range (×0.16 to ×13). Across Stage 1’s trained lags the Li+ shell and the COM g(r) do not depend on the step, but diffusion slows by 19–44 % and atom-level strain grows at long steps. Density, diffusion and the Li+ shell are intensive in system size; atom-level energies are not, and rise steeply beyond the largest training systems. These frames are not yet Boltzmann-distributed: in distribution, EF’s frames remain +9.1 kJ/mol per molecule above MD frames minimised the same way, and before minimisation their configurational temperature is θ ≈ 5 instead of 1. Closing this gap requires a Boltzmann finishing step, such as Metropolis-adjusted sampling under the full force field at fixed centres of mass, whose result θ can verify directly.

candidates.title: Evidence-Gated Plasticity and Context-Dependent Consolidation for Multi-Goal Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
candidates.abstract: Background / Introduction: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks offer a mechanistic framework for adaptive behavior, yet learning multiple goals remains challenging when synaptic updates for different targets interfere. We investigated whether multi-timescale plasticity and context-dependent consolidation improve interleaved multi-goal learning in a spiking navigation system inspired by entorhinal-hippocampal circuitry. Methods: We introduce evidence-gated plasticity (EGP), in which STDP-based reinforcement learning (STDP/RL) generates transient synaptic proposals and need-weighted behavioral evidence modulates their slower consolidation into durable weights. Global EGP pools these proposals and the corresponding evidence across goals. Target-context EGP extends this framework through goal-specific proposal and evidence stores and additional need-dependent scaling of consolidation. We compared the algorithms across paired spiking networks, tested learned weights with plasticity disabled, and examined upstream representations and consolidation components. Results: Global EGP supported multi-goal learning and durable navigation, while target-context EGP improved reward acquisition across replicated network comparisons and increased target-contact success during extended training. Independent evaluation confirmed that both algorithms retained navigation competence when plasticity was disabled. Additional controls suggested that overall consolidation strength contributes to the target-context reward advantage. In matched short-training experiments, conventional STDP/RL acquired shaped reward more rapidly, whereas EGP networks achieved higher target-contact success with learned synaptic weights held fixed. Conclusions: EGP supports durable multi-goal learning in spiking neural networks, and its target-context extension improves acquisition and conditional target selectivity in this interleaved navigation task. The framework offers a basis for testing context-sensitive, evidence-modulated plasticity in other multi-context learning problems.

candidates.title: Late-Stage Fluorosulfurylation Using Sulfuryl Fluoride Bound within a Metal–Organic Framework
candidates.abstract: Abstract Organic S(VI) fluorides have garnered substantial interest for covalent drug discovery and chemoproteomics due to their ambient stability and unique electrophilic reactivity. Sulfuryl fluoride (SO2F2) is the ideal reagent for the synthesis of various S(VI)–F moieties, yet it is a toxic greenhouse gas, often making it incompatible with laboratory settings. Developing a strategy for handling SO2F2 that is amenable to high-throughput reaction discovery would enhance its utility in the laboratory without necessitating specialized equipment or extensive safety measures. Herein, we report a strategy to safely store reactive SO2F2 within a metal–organic framework (MOF) for its facile application to the synthesis of electrophilic, bioactive molecules. The solid SO2F2–Mg2(dobdc) reagent can be stored for at least five months with minimal gas loss due to the strong yet reversible interaction between SO2F2 and Mg2+ centers in the MOF, as confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Using this reagent, we prepare a range of drug-like arylfluorosulfates, primary and secondary acyclic sulfamoyl fluorides, saturated N-heterocyclic sulfamoyl fluorides, and N-heteroarene sulfamoyl fluorides, the last of which cannot be accessed using sulfonium salt alternatives to SO2F2 due to the requirement for strongly basic conditions. These findings represent the first experimental study of SO2F2 adsorption within a MOF and the first use of MOFs for late-stage fluorosulfurylation, paving the way toward a general approach to carefully handling dangerous, reactive gases as solid reagents.

candidates.title: Machine learning-guided discovery and preliminary biological evaluation of novel GSK-3β inhibitory scaffolds with anti-inflammatory potential
candidates.abstract: Abstract This research presents an efficient machine learning-based computational pipeline aimed at the discovery of novel Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3β (GSK-3β) inhibitors. A Random Forest (RF) classification model was created using a carefully chosen set of confirmed inhibitors from 2016 to 2024. The optimized RF model was very strong and accurate (Accuracy: 0.89; AUC-ROC: 0.91 ± 0.02), making it a great first filter for finding chemicals in large spaces. We using this classifier on a new library (Asinex) to obtain the promising candidates, which then went through a series of steps, including ADMET filtering, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The pipeline found two good candidates, RF03 and RF05. In vitro enzymatic assays demonstrated moderate GSK-3β target engagement, producing IC₅₀ values of 85.04 µM and 58.73 µM, respectively. The most important thing is that the lead hit, RF05, which has a non-classical, sterically hindered aromatic ester scaffold, worked very well at the cellular level. More biological tests showed that RF05 greatly lowers the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-6) while keeping low cytotoxicity. We suggest that this unique chemotype's high lipophilicity and structural pre-organization make it easier for cells to pass through membranes and build up inside cells, turning a moderate biochemical affinity into a strong phenotypic response. This validated computational strategy significantly reduces experimental attrition. Compound RF05 is a potential lead scaffold that gives a structurally different base for the rational design of new anti-inflammatory drugs.

candidates.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Topology-Aware Modeling of Multispecific Antibody Function
candidates.abstract: Multispecific antibodies (msAbs) offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce Synapse, a biologically inspired synthetic benchmark for topology-aware modeling of msAbs. First, we present a generative method that combines nonlinear per-domain sequence-to-score landscapes with connectivity-dependent synthetic readouts. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to the evaluated connectivity-agnostic multilayer perceptron. We demonstrate that this model learns topology-dependent structure-function relationships on synthetic landscapes and evaluate a transfer learning workflow as infrastructure for adaptation to biological datasets. We showcase our framework with a trispecific T cell engager-inspired synthetic topology-dependent optimization task and a constrained ranking of common light chain candidates against a composite objective. This work provides a controlled benchmarking environment for developing and evaluating topology-aware computational tools for msAb modeling. All experiments use synthetic data; no biological validation is performed.

candidates.title: Learning from SILCS FragMaps: Combining Physics-Based Energies with Artificial Intelligence for Rapid Drug Permeability Prediction
candidates.abstract: Abstract Prediction of drug passive permeability represents an important component of rational drug design, requiring continued development of methods to address this problem. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have long been shown to be of utility for prediction of compound permeability, though they are limited by the range of chemical space in the data sets used in the training of the models. To address this, in the present study, the site identification of ligand competitive saturation (SILCS) methodology is used to calculate free energy profiles for compounds across 3 model lipid bilayers: a POPC–cholesterol bilayer, a bilayer model mimicking parallel artificial membrane permeability assay (PAMPA) experiments, and a bilayer modeling the blood–brain barrier. We present a rapid workflow generating around 15,000 such profiles that accounts for the passive permeation of more than 2500 unique ligands for 3 different membranes. The free energy profiles, which account for all accessible protonation states of the compounds, are then used as features in a collection of AI models. As the physics-based free energy profiles are calculated based on the functional group types in the compounds combined with the SILCS FragMaps calculated for the bilayers, their use potentially improves model transferability by overcoming the limitation of the applicability of the AI models to the chemical space included in the training set, assuming the SILCS-based energies are representative of barriers to compound permeabilities. The resulting models are shown to be almost comparable with available passive permeability models reported in the literature while additionally offering energetic information about the contribution of functional groups to the permeation barriers that may be used for rational compound optimization. Limitations in the cell-based training data, including the presence of drug transporters, are discussed.

candidates.title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
candidates.abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

candidates.title: Accelerated Online Risk-Averse Policy Evaluation in POMDPs with Theoretical Guarantees and Novel CVaR Bounds
candidates.abstract: Background: Risk-averse decision-making under partial observability involves evaluating a risk measure, such as the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), of the cumulative return, a computationally demanding task in POMDPs. Objectives: This work introduces a framework for accelerating CVaR value function evaluation by replacing the original POMDP dynamics with a computationally tractable surrogate model while providing formal performance guarantees. Methods: As the mathematical foundation, we derive bounds on the CVaR of a random variable X using an auxiliary random variable Y under assumptions relating their cumulative distribution functions. We introduce a truncation decomposition that separates CVaR estimation from n samples into a data-driven term -- bounded at rate O(1/√n) without support knowledge -- and a tail correction where the support bound enters only through an O(1/n) term, strictly improving existing concentration bounds. These bounds are further tightened via local CDF concentration parameters that exploit the quantile structure of CVaR. Building on this foundation, we establish upper and lower bounds on the CVaR value function computable from a simplified belief-MDP, accommodating general simplifications of the transition dynamics. We develop sample-based estimators for computing these bounds during online policy evaluation with probabilistic performance guarantees. These bounds enable computational acceleration via action elimination: actions whose bounds indicate suboptimality under the simplified model are safely discarded while ensuring consistency with the original POMDP. Results: Empirical evaluation across multiple POMDP domains confirms that the bounds reliably distinguish safe from dangerous policies while achieving 9-21× computational speedups on the evaluated benchmarks. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides a principled and practical approach for accelerating risk-averse policy evaluation in POMDPs, with theoretical guarantees and significant computational gains demonstrated across multiple domains.

candidates.title: DeePEn - A Depth sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering
candidates.abstract: Recent progress in modeling techniques and high-throughput screening has significantly enhanced the accessibility of protein engineering. Nevertheless, further progress gets hindered by the lack of robust benchmarks that capture the practical challenges for real-world protein engineering. Here, we introduced DeePEn, a Depth-sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering that quantifies model generalization to held-out variants at increasing mutational distance from the wild type. We defined distance as the number of simultaneous point mutations, i.e., single amino acid variants (SAVs), moving from wild-type to mutant (edit distance in computer science jargon). DeePEn retrospectively evaluates prediction and prioritization using experimentally labelled variants from deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets; it does not benchmark prospective sequence generation or goal-directed optimization. Specifically selecting four DMS datasets with sufficient multi-mutation data points from ProteinGym, we assessed recent predictive models, including general and biophysics-informed protein Language Models (pLMs), and a non-transformer neural network. Our results highlight how the performance of all models deteriorates with increasing mutational distance and that no single metric sufficiently captures the diverse requirements of protein engineering. To overcome these shortcomings, DeePEn provides a readily available resource for multi-metric benchmarking that focuses on variant-effect prediction of variants distant from the wild type.

candidates.title: Multi-objective optimization of speed-sensorless sliding mode vector control for electric motors based on HSMO and MOGA
candidates.abstract: Purpose Speed-sensorless induction-motor drives are limited by low-speed flux-estimation errors, parameter mismatch, and sliding-mode chattering. This study proposes a hybrid sliding-mode observer-based optimized control (HSMO-OC) framework to improve speed estimation, dynamic response, and electromagnetic-output smoothness. Methods A hybrid sliding-mode observer (HSMO) combines voltage-model and current-model flux estimates using speed-dependent weighting and continuous sliding-mode correction. A multi-objective genetic algorithm (MOGA) jointly optimizes observer and sliding-mode speed-controller parameters under stability and engineering constraints. MATLAB/Simulink simulations of a 2.2 kW induction-motor drive compare four control configurations under startup, speed transitions, load disturbances, low-speed operation, and three uncertainty conditions. Results Compared with the conventional SMO-SMC baseline, HSMO-OC reduced speed root-mean-square error from 28.9 to 9.6 r/min, settling time from 0.204 to 0.109 s, and load-induced speed drop from 64.8 to 21.5 r/min. Torque-ripple and current-ripple RMS values decreased from 0.96 to 0.41 N·m and from 1.07 to 0.48 A, respectively. At 100 r/min, speed RMSE was 2.8 r/min. Under resistance mismatch, measurement noise, and inverter dead time, speed RMSE values were 13.4, 12.7, and 14.2 r/min, respectively. Conclusion The results demonstrate the complementary contributions of hybrid flux observation and joint multi-objective parameter optimization to estimation accuracy, disturbance rejection, and electromagnetic-output smoothness under the tested simulation conditions.

candidates.title: Toward precision nanomedicine via artificial intelligence guided design and prediction.
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

candidates.title: Traffic density-aware multi-objective edge server deployment for vehicular edge computing
candidates.abstract: Vehicular edge computing (VEC) has been introduced as a promising paradigm to support latency-sensitive and computation-intensive vehicular applications. However, the dynamic mobility of vehicles and uneven traffic distribution bring great challenges in efficient edge server deployment. Inappropriate positioning of the edge servers may increase the communication latency, energy consumption, service interruptions, and handover frequency and thus degrade the overall network performance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a traffic density-aware multi-objective edge server deployment framework for VEC environments based on the traffic density-aware non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (TDA-NSGA-II). The proposed framework exploits realistic simulation of urban mobility (SUMO)-generated vehicular mobility traces to identify high-density traffic regions and optimize edge server locations accordingly. The optimization process jointly minimizes communication latency and energy consumption while improving coverage and reducing handovers. In addition, the proposed scheme implements mobility-aware vehicle-to-server association to provide stable connectivity under dynamic vehicular movement. Experimental evaluations are conducted based on realistic traffic mobility scenarios and compared with conventional optimization approaches such as genetic algorithm (GA), particle swarm optimization (PSO) and ant colony optimization (ACO). Simulation results presented in this paper demonstrate that the proposed TDA-NSGA-II framework achieves substantially lower latency and energy consumption than GA, PSO and ACO, with coverage comparable to the best baseline, while handover counts remain comparable rather than consistently reduced. The results illustrate that traffic-density-aware edge server deployment can significantly improve the efficiency and reliability of VEC networks. The proposed framework provides an effective solution for adaptive edge server deployment in dynamic vehicular edge computing environments and can support latency-sensitive intelligent transportation applications through efficient resource utilization and improved communication reliability.

candidates.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.
